overview: Baden grew from divided margraviates into a much larger grand duchy along the Upper Rhine. Karlsruhe became an important capital, while Mannheim and other towns developed manufacturing and new transport. The imported 1715 to 1878 outline is misleading at its early dates: it projects a later, enlarged territory backward over lands Baden acquired much later. The grand duchy itself continued until 1918.

periods.title: Divided Baden
periods.summary: Baden-Durlach and Baden-Baden remained separate until their dynastic reunion.

periods.title: Union and expansion
periods.summary: The reunited margraviate expanded greatly during the Napoleonic reordering of Germany.

periods.title: The grand duchy
periods.summary: Baden became a grand duchy; its monarchy ended in the revolution of 1918.

sections.title: Building a state and a capital

items.text: In 1771, Karl Friedrich of Baden-Durlach inherited Baden-Baden, joining Protestant and Catholic territories under one ruler. Further acquisitions between 1802 and 1810 included Heidelberg, Mannheim and lands farther south. The familiar long shape of Baden emerged through these changes, rather than existing unchanged in 1715.

Karlsruhe’s founding offer in 1715 welcomed settlers of different Christian denominations. Such promises helped a new town attract inhabitants, but everyday equality remained contested: religious communities still argued over their treatment and public rights. A ruler’s invitation was the beginning of negotiations about living together.

Baden’s expanded territory brought together places with different legal traditions. Johann Niklas Friedrich Brauer adapted the French civil code into a Baden law book. Announced in 1808, a uniform civil law finally took effect in 1810. Governing a bigger state required more than drawing a larger border.

sections.title: A constitution in its own words

items.text: Writing sample: section 14 of the constitution of 22 August 1818 says, “Die Gerichte sind unabhängig innerhalb der Grenzen ihrer Competenz.” It means “The courts are independent within the limits of their jurisdiction.” This German wording, including the spelling Competenz, comes from a modern transcription of the historical document.

The same constitution protected property and personal liberty and provided two parliamentary chambers. Its rights were unequal: eligibility for the second chamber required being Christian, at least thirty, and meeting financial qualifications. Reading both the promises and the exclusions helps explain why constitutional reform did not finish the struggle for political rights.

sections.title: Light, water and the awkward business of toilets

items.text: Karlsruhe’s first public oil lamps appeared in 1759. They burned rapeseed oil and were lit only on moonless nights when the margrave was present. The moon had a surprisingly important job in the lighting budget, and a ruler’s absence could leave everyone relying on it.

In 1764, a new Karlsruhe waterworks used horses to drive wooden pumping machinery. It lifted groundwater from about three metres below ground. Keeping water moving required animals, mechanisms and maintenance long before electric pumps could be switched on.

After the map’s 1878 cutoff, but still during the grand duchy, Karlsruhe expanded its sewers from 1883. Toilets did not immediately join them: water closets were expensive for working families, and officials worried about fouling the river. Cesspits remained part of the system; in 1893 officials permitted sewer expansion for flushing away human waste. Underground pipes alone did not solve the toilet question.

On 12 June 1817, Karl von Drais rode his running machine from Mannheim toward Schwetzingen and back, covering about fourteen kilometres in a little over an hour. Riders pushed against the ground with their feet. Pedals were still in the future: the engine was the person sitting on top.

These early machines were largely wooden, with a few iron parts. Drais sold construction plans that craftsmen turned into vehicles. A wheelwright’s workshop, rather than a modern bicycle factory, supplied the skills behind this invention’s first examples.

Food prices made 1817 much harder for families than the bicycle story suggests. After the disastrous harvest of 1816, a one-kreuzer bread roll in Mannheim shrank from seven Loth to two and a half Loth, roughly 112 grams to 40 grams. The price stayed the same while the portion became much smaller.

Johann Peter Hebel turned calendar writing into memorable literature. His 1811 Schatzkästlein collected 127 short pieces from earlier issues of the Rheinländischer Hausfreund. He revised expressions for readers beyond the local dialect area. A calendar could offer stories and observations alongside its practical job of marking the year.

When Prussian troops bombarded Rastatt in July 1849, civilians took shelter in cellars, the palace and fortifications. The revolutionary stronghold surrendered on 23 July. Captivity and disease followed for prisoners. The struggle over government reached homes and families as well as soldiers and political leaders.

ending.text: Grand Duke Friedrich II definitively renounced the throne on 22 November 1918, after a provisional government had formed. Baden changed from a monarchy into a republic. Its people, towns and institutions continued; the imported map endpoint of 1878 does not mark the end of the state.
